title: Solving on a Restricted Interval
subject: mathematics

theory.introduction: A restricted interval limits the set of acceptable solutions. Unlike a general solution, where every possible value is represented using an integer parameter, a restricted-interval problem asks you to find only the solutions that lie inside a specified range. The main skills are reading the interval correctly, finding all trigonometric solutions, using the unit circle and reference angles, handling endpoints correctly, and checking that every answer belongs to the requested interval.

content.text: A restricted interval tells you exactly which values of x are allowed. For example, 0 ≤ x < 2π means that x may be 0 but may not be 2π.
A solution to the trigonometric equation is valid only if it satisfies both the equation and the specified interval.
The same equation can therefore have infinitely many solutions in general but only a finite number of solutions on a restricted interval.
Common intervals include 0 ≤ x < 2π and 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
Common radian intervals include 0 ≤ x < 2π, 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π, −π ≤ x ≤ π, and 0 ≤ x ≤ π.
Common degree intervals include 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°, 0° ≤ x < 360°, −180° ≤ x ≤ 180°, and 0° ≤ x ≤ 180°.
Always read whether each endpoint is included. The symbols ≤ and < are important.

Common intervals include 0 ≤ x < 2π, 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π, and 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°. The basic trigonometric equation methods are taught in trig-equations-03; this lesson focuses on selecting every valid solution inside the stated interval.
Use the unit circle, reference angles, and periodicity to identify every solution inside the required interval.
Trigonometric equations may be expressed in degrees or radians. Do not mix the two systems within a calculation.
A complete revolution is 360° or 2π radians. Therefore 180° = π radians.
Before solving, identify the unit used by the equation and the interval.
Use the degree/radian definitions from degrees-and-radians. Here the only new task is applying the correct full-turn period while filtering solutions in the requested interval.

Use the unit circle as a lookup and selection tool. The basic equation lesson determines what trigonometric value is required; this lesson determines which angles in the requested interval produce that value.
The objective is interval filtering, not a second derivation of the coordinate definitions of sine, cosine, and tangent.

sections.title: Reference Angles as a Solution-Selection Tool

content.text: Reference angles and quadrant signs were developed in the any-angle trigonometric-ratios lesson. Here they are used only as a procedure for locating solutions after a basic equation has been solved.

For an equation such as sin x = a, first determine the reference angle and then select the quadrants in which sine has the required sign. Do not treat this section as a second lesson on constructing reference angles from scratch.

Use the established quadrant sign rules to choose the correct terminal positions for a solution. The full coordinate-plane explanation and CAST/ASTC reasoning belong to trigonometric-ratios-any-angle.
In this lesson, the sign table is a decision aid: sine is positive in Quadrants I and II, cosine in I and IV, and tangent in I and III.

sections.title: Solving Sine Equations on a Restricted Interval

content.text: For a sine equation, first use the basic solution method from trig-equations-03 to identify the branches. Then list only the values inside the specified interval.

sections.title: Solving Cosine Equations on a Restricted Interval

content.text: For a cosine equation, first use the basic solution method from trig-equations-03. Then generate and filter all valid angles in the interval.

sections.title: Solving Tangent Equations on a Restricted Interval

content.text: For a tangent equation, use its π or 180° periodicity from the basic-equation framework, generate all candidates in the interval, and discard anything outside the bounds.
For sec, csc, and cot, first rewrite and solve using trig-equations-04. Then apply the interval-filtering method here while preserving the reciprocal function domain restrictions.
If the equation contains nx, the interval must be transformed before generating solutions.
For example, if 0 ≤ x < 2π and the equation contains 3x, then 0 ≤ 3x < 6π.
Solve for 3x across the entire transformed interval, then divide each valid solution by 3.
This prevents solutions from being missed.
Some problems use intervals such as −π ≤ x ≤ π. In these cases, negative angles must be considered directly.
Use the even and odd properties of cosine and sine when useful: cos(−x) = cos(x) and sin(−x) = −sin(x).
Tangent is also odd: tan(−x) = −tan(x).
An endpoint written with ≤ is included; an endpoint written with < is excluded.
For example, 0 ≤ x < 2π includes 0 but excludes 2π.

Because many trigonometric functions repeat at the endpoints of a full revolution, including both 0 and 2π can sometimes represent the same point twice. Follow the exact interval given rather than automatically including both.
Always test endpoint values in the original equation when there is any doubt.
A reliable procedure is: identify the function, find the reference angle or principal angle, determine the valid quadrants, generate all angles in the interval, and finally verify the answers.
For multiple-angle equations, first transform the interval and solve for the complete multiple angle before converting back to x.
Do not stop after finding the first angle returned by a calculator.
The unit-circle angles 0, π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2 and their related angles are especially important for exact restricted-interval solutions.
Memorizing the standard sine, cosine, and tangent values allows many equations to be solved without a calculator.
A calculator can provide a principal inverse-trigonometric value, but it does not automatically provide every solution in a restricted interval.
Use the principal value as a starting point, then generate the other solutions using symmetry, reference angles, or the general solution.
Check that the calculator is in degree mode for degree problems and radian mode for radian problems.
Substitute each final value into the original equation.
Also verify that every answer belongs to the specified interval.
For equations involving reciprocals or multiple-angle expressions, checking the original equation is particularly important.
Substitute final values into the original equation and verify that each belongs to the stated interval. More detailed transformation-related checking belongs to trig-equations-10.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] One Full Revolution
formulas.explanation: One complete revolution can be represented using either degrees or radians.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Degree-Radian Conversion
formulas.explanation: Use this relationship to convert between degrees and radians.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Degrees to Radians
formulas.explanation: Multiply a degree measure by π/180 to convert it to radians.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Radians to Degrees
formulas.explanation: Multiply a radian measure by 180/π to convert it to degrees.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine General Solution
formulas.expression: sin(x) = a  ⇒  x = sin⁻¹(a) + 2nπ  OR  x = π − sin⁻¹(a) + 2nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Generate the complete sine solution set first, then retain only values inside the requested interval.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Compact Sine Solution
formulas.expression: sin(x) = a  ⇒  x = (−1)ⁿsin⁻¹(a) + nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: A compact form representing both families of sine solutions.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine General Solution
formulas.explanation: Use both signs and then select the values inside the restricted interval.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent General Solution
formulas.expression: tan(x) = a  ⇒  x = tan⁻¹(a) + nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Tangent repeats every π, so one solution family with n ∈ ℤ generates all solutions.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Equal Sine Rule
formulas.expression: sin(x) = sin(θ)  ⇒  x = θ + 2nπ  OR  x = π − θ + 2nπ
formulas.explanation: The two families account for the two sine solutions in each 2π cycle.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Equal Cosine Rule
formulas.explanation: The ± accounts for cosine's symmetry about the x-axis.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Equal Tangent Rule
formulas.explanation: Tangent repeats every π.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Positive and Negative Sine
formulas.expression: sin(x) > 0 in Quadrants I and II; sin(x) < 0 in Quadrants III and IV
formulas.explanation: Use the sign to determine which quadrants contain solutions.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Positive and Negative Cosine
formulas.expression: cos(x) > 0 in Quadrants I and IV; cos(x) < 0 in Quadrants II and III
formulas.explanation: Use the sign to determine which quadrants contain solutions.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Positive and Negative Tangent
formulas.expression: tan(x) > 0 in Quadrants I and III; tan(x) < 0 in Quadrants II and IV
formulas.explanation: Use the sign to determine the quadrants for tangent solutions.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine Period
formulas.explanation: Sine repeats every 2π.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine Period
formulas.explanation: Cosine repeats every 2π.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent Period
formulas.explanation: Tangent repeats every π.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine Symmetry
formulas.explanation: Sine is an odd function and changes sign for negative angles.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine Symmetry
formulas.explanation: Cosine is an even function.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent Symmetry
formulas.explanation: Tangent is an odd function.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine Reference Angle
formulas.explanation: The positive acute angle α can be used as the reference angle when solving sin(x) = a.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine Reference Angle
formulas.explanation: The positive acute angle α can be used as the reference angle when solving cos(x) = a.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent Reference Angle
formulas.explanation: The positive acute angle α can be used as the reference angle when solving tan(x) = a.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Multiple-Angle Interval Transformation
formulas.expression: If θ = nx and a ≤ x < b, then for n > 0: na ≤ θ < nb
formulas.explanation: Transform the interval before solving equations involving nx so that no solutions are missed.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Period of sin(nx)
formulas.explanation: A larger coefficient creates more cycles over the same x-interval.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Period of cos(nx)
formulas.explanation: Use this to understand solution spacing and solution count.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Period of tan(nx)
formulas.explanation: Tangent completes a cycle over π in its input, so tan(nx) has x-period π/|n|.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Secant Reciprocal Identity
formulas.explanation: Use this to convert secant equations into cosine equations.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosecant Reciprocal Identity
formulas.explanation: Use this to convert cosecant equations into sine equations.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cotangent Reciprocal Identity
formulas.explanation: Use this to convert cotangent equations into tangent equations when appropriate.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Sine Zero Solutions
formulas.explanation: Use the interval to select the valid values.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Cosine Zero Solutions
formulas.expression: cos(x) = 0  ⇒  x = π/2 + nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Use the interval to select the valid values.

formulas.name: [IMPORTANT FOR PROBLEM SOLVING] Tangent Zero Solutions
formulas.explanation: Use the interval to select the valid values.

formulas.explanation: These unit-circle values are frequently used for exact restricted-interval solutions.

examples.question: Solve cos(x) = 1/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/3. Cosine is positive in Quadrants I and IV, giving x = π/3 and 5π/3.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) = 1/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/6. Sine is positive in Quadrants I and II. Therefore x = π/6 and 5π/6.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) = −1/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/6. Sine is negative in Quadrants III and IV. Therefore x = 7π/6 and 11π/6.

examples.question: Solve cos(x) = −√3/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/6. Cosine is negative in Quadrants II and III. Therefore x = 5π/6 and 7π/6.

examples.question: Solve tan(x) = 1 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/4. Tangent is positive in Quadrants I and III. Therefore x = π/4 and 5π/4.

examples.question: Solve sec(x) = 2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Rewrite as cos(x) = 1/2. The solutions are x = π/3 and 5π/3.

examples.question: Solve csc(x) = −1 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Rewrite as sin(x) = −1. Sine equals −1 at x = 3π/2, which is the only solution in 0 ≤ x < 2π.

examples.question: Solve cot(x) = 1 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Since cot(x) = 1/tan(x), tan(x) = 1. Tangent is positive in Quadrants I and III, giving x = π/4 and 5π/4.

examples.question: Solve sin(2x) = 1/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Let θ = 2x. Then 0 ≤ θ < 4π. Solve sin(θ) = 1/2: θ = π/6, 5π/6, 13π/6, 17π/6. Dividing by 2 gives x = π/12, 5π/12, 13π/12, 17π/12.

examples.question: Solve cos(3x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Let θ = 3x. Then 0 ≤ θ < 6π. Since cos(θ) = 0, θ = π/2 + nπ. The six values in the transformed interval are π/2, 3π/2, 5π/2, 7π/2, 9π/2, 11π/2. Dividing by 3 gives x = π/6, π/2, 5π/6, 7π/6, 3π/2, 11π/6.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) = −√2/2 for −π ≤ x ≤ π.
examples.solution: The reference angle is π/4. In the interval −π ≤ x ≤ π, sin(x) is −√2/2 at x = −3π/4 and −π/4.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π.
examples.solution: Sine is zero at integer multiples of π. In this closed interval, x = 0, π, and 2π. If the interval were 0 ≤ x < 2π, then 2π would be excluded.

examples.question: Solve cos(x) = 1/2 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
examples.solution: The reference angle is 60°. Cosine is positive in Quadrants I and IV, giving x = 60° and 300°.

examples.question: Solve sin(x) = −√3/2 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
examples.solution: The reference angle is 60°. Sine is negative in Quadrants III and IV, giving x = 240° and 300°.

examples.question: Solve cos(2x + π/3) = 1/2 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Let θ = 2x + π/3. Then cos(θ) = 1/2, so θ = ±π/3 + 2nπ. Solve both families: 2x + π/3 = π/3 + 2nπ gives x = nπ; and 2x + π/3 = −π/3 + 2nπ gives x = −π/3 + nπ. Select the values in 0 ≤ x < 2π. The solutions are x = 0, π, 2π/3, and 5π/3.

examples.question: How many solutions does sin(3x) = 0 have for 0 ≤ x < 2π?
examples.solution: sin(3x) = 0 gives 3x = nπ, so x = nπ/3. The interval 0 ≤ x < 2π gives n = 0,1,2,3,4,5. Therefore there are 6 solutions: 0, π/3, 2π/3, π, 4π/3, and 5π/3.

key_ideas: A restricted interval determines which solutions are valid.
Always read the endpoint symbols carefully.
Use the unit circle for exact special-angle solutions.
Use reference angles together with quadrant signs for non-special values.
A calculator's inverse trigonometric function normally returns only a principal value.
Sine has period 2π, cosine has period 2π, and tangent has period π.
For multiple-angle equations, transform the interval before solving.
Generate every possible solution before filtering by the original interval.
For reciprocal functions, rewrite using reciprocal identities when useful.
Check the final solutions in the original equation.
Do not confuse degrees and radians.
The interval 0 ≤ x < 2π does not include 2π, while 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π does.
A general solution and a restricted-interval solution are different forms of the answer.
The safest workflow is: solve completely, restrict, then verify.
misconceptions: Giving a general solution when the question asks for solutions in a restricted interval.
Using only the principal inverse-trigonometric value.
Finding only one quadrant instead of all valid quadrants.
Forgetting that negative trigonometric values occur in different quadrants.
Excluding an endpoint that is actually included.
Automatically listing both 0 and 2π when the interval is 0 ≤ x < 2π.
Using degree answers for a radian interval.
Using radian answers for a degree interval.
Forgetting to transform the interval for equations involving 2x, 3x, or another multiple angle.
Dividing a multiple-angle equation too early and losing solutions.
Ignoring domain restrictions for tangent and reciprocal functions.
Failing to check the final answers in the original equation.
